source_text: Ut enim imaginem Dei mentis ratione suscepimus; ita communionem pecudum carnis affinitate sentimus; cuius licet sit forma diversa, est tamen de materia elementorum una substantia; pro rationabilis sane animi meritis aeternitatem visura, vel aerumnis miseram, vel praemiis gloriosam.
pass_a_gloss: For as we received the image of God by the reason of the mind; so we feel the communion of cattle by the affinity of flesh; of which, although the form is diverse, there is nevertheless one substance from the matter of the elements; about to see eternity according to the deserts of a rational mind, either miserable with hardships or glorious with rewards.

lemmas.lexica: LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS meritum; Blaise; glossary: desert not treasury-of-merit

pass_b_english: Just as we received God’s image through the reason of the mind (compare Genesis 1:26–27), so we experience our kinship with cattle through the affinity of the flesh. Although its form differs, its substance, drawn from the material of the elements, is one. Our flesh will indeed see eternity according to the merits of the rational soul: either miserable in suffering or glorious in rewards (Genesis 1:26–27).

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
